title: श्रीमद्भगवद्गीता — कर्मसंन्यासयोगः
titleEn: The Bhagavad Gītā — Chapter 5: The Renunciation of Action
draftNote: Prepared by the Lectorium pipeline from the vulgate text, with a drafting pass, a reviewing pass and a mechanical gate; a printed-edition collation and audio are still to come. Use ⚑ correction on any verse to report a problem.

sentences.l: Renunciation of-actions, O Kṛṣṇa, and again yoga, you-praise; which of-these-two [is] the-one better — that to-me tell, well-ascertained.
sentences.i: You praise renunciation of actions, Kṛṣṇa, and also yoga; tell me decisively which of the two is better.
sentences.n: Arjuna reopens the question chapter 3 seemed to have closed: saṃnyāsa, 'renunciation [of action]', against karma-yoga, both of which Kṛṣṇa has praised (in ch. 3 and 4) without ranking. Śreyaḥ, 'better', repeats the term from 2.7's opening plea (yac chreyaḥ syān niścitam); suniścitam, 'well-ascertained, decisively', asks for a definite answer, not further ambiguity.

sentences.l: Renunciation and the-yoga-of-action, both productive-of-the-highest-good; of-these-two, however, than-renunciation-of-action, the-yoga-of-action excels.
sentences.i: Renunciation and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good; but of the two, the yoga of action excels renunciation of action.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa's direct answer to verse 1: both paths lead to niḥśreyasa, 'the highest good' (an intensified form of the śreyaḥ just asked about), but karma-saṃnyāsāt karma-yogaḥ viśiṣyate, 'the yoga of action excels renunciation of action' — an ablative of comparison. This verdict is qualified through the rest of the chapter: verse 6 explains why (renunciation is hard without yoga first), and verses 4-5 will insist the two are not really separate in their fruit.

sentences.l: To-be-known [is] he [as] the-eternal-renouncer who not hates, not desires; free-from-the-pairs-of-opposites, indeed, O great-armed-one, easily from-bondage he-is-released.
sentences.i: One who neither hates nor desires should be known as the true, ever-renouncing man; free from the pairs of opposites, great-armed one, he is easily released from bondage.
sentences.n: This redefines saṃnyāsin, 'renouncer', in inward rather than outward terms: not one who abstains from acts, but one na dveṣṭi na kāṅkṣati, 'who neither hates nor desires' — the same freedom from attraction and aversion praised at 2.64. Nirdvandvaḥ, 'free from the pairs of opposites' (cf. 4.22's dvandvātītaḥ), names the state that makes such a person 'easily released from bondage', quietly answering verse 2's ranking: this is what karma-yoga itself aims at.

sentences.l: Sāṃkhya-and-yoga separately fools declare, not the-wise; one even having-taken-his-stand-in, fully, of-both, one-obtains the-fruit.
sentences.i: Fools speak of sāṃkhya and yoga as different, not the wise; one who has truly taken his stand in even one of them obtains the fruit of both.
sentences.n: Sāṃkhya and yoga are kept untranslated per convention, as the poem's two named paths (from 3.3 on); this verse insists they are not opposed schools but two doors to the same result — whoever is truly established (samyak āsthitaḥ) in either 'obtains the fruit of both' (ubhayor vindate phalam), a claim developed concretely in verse 5.

sentences.l: Which by-followers-of-sāṃkhya is-attained, the-state, that by-followers-of-yoga also is-reached; sāṃkhya and yoga as-one who sees, he [truly] sees.

sentences.n: The Wikisource page misprints a stray ASCII colon after स in the second line ("स: पश्यति"); the corrected reading, matching BORI, is स पश्यति, 'he [truly] sees', adopted here. The doubled paśyati ... paśyati ('sees ... sees') is emphatic: only one who sees sāṃkhya and yoga as leading to the same sthānam, 'state', truly sees, completing the claim of verse 4.

sentences.l: Renunciation, however, O great-armed-one, is-difficult to-attain without-yoga; disciplined-by-yoga, the-sage, brahman, without-delay, reaches.
sentences.i: But renunciation, great-armed one, is hard to attain without yoga; the sage disciplined in yoga reaches brahman before long.
sentences.n: This qualifies verse 2's ranking: saṃnyāsa itself, far from being easier, is duḥkham āptum ayogataḥ, 'hard to attain without yoga' — i.e. karma-yoga is the very means by which true renunciation (as redefined in verse 3) becomes possible. Only the yoga-yuktaḥ muniḥ, 'the sage disciplined in yoga', reaches brahman nacireṇa, 'before long, without delay'.

sentences.l: Disciplined-by-yoga, of-purified-mind, of-conquered-self, of-conquered-senses; whose-self-has-become-the-self-of-all-beings — even doing, not is-he-stained.
sentences.i: Disciplined in yoga, his mind purified, his self conquered, his senses mastered, his very self become the self of all beings — even while acting, he is not stained.
sentences.n: A five-fold nominative description builds the portrait of the ideal karma-yogin, culminating in sarva-bhūta-ātma-bhūta-ātmā, 'whose self has become the self of all beings' — a striking claim of identity with all creatures that anticipates the equal vision of verses 18-19. Kurvann api na lipyate, 'even acting, he is not stained', restates 3.9's teaching that action itself does not bind, and is developed by the lotus-leaf simile of verse 10.

sentences.l: Not-at-all 'anything I-do' thus disciplined should-think the-knower-of-truth — seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing,
sentences.i: The disciplined knower of truth should think, 'I do nothing at all' — even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing,
sentences.n: The Wikisource source misprints the second line's opening participle with an extra र् as श्रृण्वन्; the corrected reading, matching BORI, is शृण्वन् (śṛṇvan, 'hearing'), adopted here. Yuktaḥ ... manyeta, 'the disciplined man should think', is an optative main clause governing the quoted thought naiva kiṃcit karomi, 'I do nothing at all'; the string of present participles that follows (continuing without a break into verse 9) names the ordinary bodily and sense-functions such a person still performs while holding that thought.

sentences.l: talking, excreting, grasping, opening-the-eyes, closing-the-eyes, even — 'the-senses among-the-objects-of-the-senses move' thus holding [in mind].
sentences.i: talking, excreting, grasping, opening and closing his eyes — holding always that it is the senses that move among their objects.
sentences.n: Verses 8-9 form a single sentence: the thirteen participles here complete the list of bodily activities begun in verse 8, all governed by the same yuktaḥ ... manyeta of verse 8. The concluding thought he holds, indriyāṇi indriyārtheṣu vartante, 'the senses move among their objects' (not the self), is the doctrinal point of the whole list — a Sāṃkhya-style distinction between the acting senses and the inactive self that Śaṅkara treats as the verse's real teaching.

sentences.l: In-brahman having-placed actions, attachment having-abandoned, does [them], who — is-stained not he by-sin, [as] a-lotus-leaf by-water.
sentences.i: One who acts, having placed his actions in brahman and abandoned attachment, is not stained by sin, as a lotus-leaf is not wetted by water.
sentences.n: Brahmaṇy ādhāya karmāṇi, 'having placed his actions in brahman', recalls the sacrifice-teaching of 4.24 (brahmārpaṇam) and echoes the same idea — depositing one's actions in a locus beyond the ego — as 3.30's mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi sannyasya, 'having consigned all actions to me'; the lotus-leaf simile (padma-patram iva ambhasā), one of the chapter's most memorable images, illustrates verse 7's kurvann api na lipyate in concrete terms.

sentences.t:
कायेन मनसा बुद्ध्या केवलैरिन्द्रियैरपि ।
योगिनः कर्म कुर्वन्ति सङ्गं त्यक्त्वात्मशुद्धये ॥
sentences.tr:
kāyena manasā buddhyā kevalaiḥ indriyaiḥ api |
yoginaḥ karma kurvanti saṅgam tyaktvā ātma-śuddhaye ||

morph.gloss: body (instr. sg. 'with the body')
mind (instr. sg. 'with the mind')
intellect, understanding (instr. sg. 'with the intellect')
mere, alone (instr. pl., agreeing with indriyaiḥ)
sense-organ (indriyaiḥ: instr. pl. 'with the senses'; -aiḥ + i- → -air i-)
even, also (indriyaiḥ + api → indriyair api)
one who practices yoga, a yogin (nom. pl., subject)
action (acc. sg., object of kurvanti)
to do (kurvanti: present 3rd pl.)
attachment (acc. sg., object of tyaktvā)
to abandon (tyaktvā: gerund 'having given up')
self (first compound member)
purification (ātma-śuddhi: 'purification of the self', śuddhaye: dat. sg. 'for the purification of'; tyaktvā + ā- → tyaktvā-)

sentences.l: With-the-body, with-the-mind, with-the-intellect, with-the-senses even, [when] mere — yogins action perform, attachment having-abandoned, for-self-purification.
sentences.i: Yogins perform action with body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, without attachment, for the purification of the self.
sentences.n: Kevalaiḥ indriyaiḥ, 'with the senses alone' (bare sense-activity, without ego-investment), names the minimal residue of action even the disciplined still perform, anticipating 4.21's śārīraṃ kevalaṃ karma; ātma-śuddhaye, 'for the purification of the self', gives such action's sole remaining purpose.

sentences.t:
युक्तः कर्मफलं त्यक्त्वा शान्तिमाप्नोति नैष्ठिकीम् ।
अयुक्तः कामकारेण फले सक्तो निबध्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
yuktaḥ karma-phalam tyaktvā śāntim āpnoti naiṣṭhikīm |
ayuktaḥ kāma-kāreṇa phale saktaḥ nibadhyate ||

morph.gloss: to join, discipline (yukta: past participle 'disciplined', nom. sg., subject)
action (first compound member)
fruit (karma-phala: 'the fruit of action', acc. sg., object of tyaktvā)
to abandon (tyaktvā: gerund 'having given up')
peace (śāntim: acc. sg., object of āpnoti)
to attain, reach (āpnoti: present 3rd sg.)
settled, final, resulting from steadfast devotion (derivative of niṣṭhā, 'steadfastness'; naiṣṭhikīm: acc. sg. fem., agreeing with śāntim)
undisciplined, not disciplined in yoga (nom. sg., subject)
desire (first compound member)
action, impulse (kāma-kāra: 'the impulse of desire', instr. sg. 'through the impulse of desire')
fruit (loc. sg. 'in the fruit')
to cling, be attached (sakta: past participle 'attached', nom. sg.; -aḥ before n- → -o)
to bind, fetter (nibadhyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is bound')

sentences.l: The-disciplined-one, the-fruit-of-action having-abandoned, peace attains, settled/final; the-undisciplined-one, through-the-impulse-of-desire, in-the-fruit attached, is-bound.
sentences.i: The disciplined man, having given up the fruit of action, attains lasting peace; the undisciplined man, driven by desire and attached to the fruit, is bound.
sentences.n: A direct contrast of yuktaḥ and ayuktaḥ, 'the disciplined' and 'the undisciplined', restates the house rendering of 2.47 in narrative form: giving up karma-phalam, 'the fruit of action', yields śāntim ... naiṣṭhikīm, 'lasting, settled peace', while kāma-kāreṇa phale saktaḥ, 'attached to the fruit through the impulse of desire', brings bondage.

sentences.t:
सर्वकर्माणि मनसा संन्यस्यास्ते सुखं वशी ।
नवद्वारे पुरे देही नैव कुर्वन्न कारयन् ॥
sentences.tr:
sarva-karmāṇi manasā saṃnyasya āste sukham vaśī |
nava-dvāre pure dehī na eva kurvan na kārayan ||

morph.gloss: all (first compound member)
action (sarva-karman: 'all actions', acc. pl., object of saṃnyasya)
mind (instr. sg. 'with the mind, mentally')
to renounce, lay down (saṃnyasya: gerund 'having renounced')
to sit, remain, dwell (āste: present middle 3rd sg. 'remains, abides'; saṃnyasya + ā- → saṃnyasyā-)
happily, at ease (adverbial acc. sg. neut.)
self-controlled, master of oneself (nom. sg.)
nine (first compound member)
gate, door (nava-dvāra: 'nine-gated', loc. sg., agreeing with pure)
city, citadel (loc. sg. 'in the city' — a figure for the body)
the embodied one, the possessor of a body (nom. sg., subject of āste)
not (na + e- → nai-)
at all, indeed
to do (kurvan: present participle nom. sg. 'doing')
not (kurvan + na → kurvanna, doubled n)
to do (causative kārayati: kārayan: present participle nom. sg. 'causing to be done')

sentences.l: All-actions, with-the-mind, having-renounced, dwells happily, the-self-controlled; in-the-nine-gated city, the-embodied-one, not-at-all doing, nor causing-to-be-done.
sentences.i: Having mentally renounced all actions, the self-controlled embodied self dwells happily in the nine-gated city, neither acting nor causing action.
sentences.n: Nava-dvāre pure, 'the nine-gated city', is the standard figure for the body (two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two lower openings); manasā saṃnyasya, 'having renounced with the mind', makes explicit that the renunciation meant throughout is inward, resuming the theme of verse 3 and closing the run of verses (6-13) on the true, active saṃnyāsin.

sentences.t:
न कर्तृत्वं न कर्माणि लोकस्य सृजति प्रभुः ।
न कर्मफलसंयोगं स्वभावस्तु प्रवर्तते ॥
sentences.tr:
na kartṛtvam na karmāṇi lokasya sṛjati prabhuḥ |
na karma-phala-saṃyogam svabhāvaḥ tu pravartate ||

morph.gloss: not
agent, doer (kartṛtva: 'agency, the state of being an agent', acc. sg. neut.)
not
action (acc. pl.)
world (gen. sg. 'of the world', i.e. for the beings of the world)
to create, produce (sṛjati: present 3rd sg.)
lord, master (nom. sg., subject, referring to the self)
not
action (first compound member)
fruit (second compound member)
union, connection (karma-phala-saṃyoga: 'connection with the fruit of action', acc. sg., object of sṛjati, continued from line 1)
one's own nature, inherent nature (svabhāvaḥ: nom. sg., subject; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
but, rather
to proceed, operate, come into play (pravartate: present middle 3rd sg. 'proceeds, functions')

sentences.l: Not agency, not actions, of-the-world creates the-lord; not connection-with-the-fruit-of-action — own-nature, rather, functions.
sentences.i: The self creates for the world neither agency, nor actions, nor the connection with the fruit of action; it is one's own nature that brings all this about.
sentences.n: Prabhuḥ, 'the Lord' (i.e. the self, or Kṛṣṇa as the supreme self within all), is declared uninvolved in creating agency, action, or the fruit-connection of the two; svabhāvaḥ, 'one's own [material] nature' (an individual's portion of prakṛti, cf. 3.33), is what actually 'functions' — an argument that turns from the practical ethics of verses 1-13 to the underlying metaphysics completed in verse 15.

sentences.t:
नादत्ते कस्यचित्पापं न चैव सुकृतं विभुः ।
अज्ञानेनावृतं ज्ञानं तेन मुह्यन्ति जन्तवः ॥
sentences.tr:
na ādatte kasyacit pāpam na ca eva sukṛtam vibhuḥ |
ajñānena āvṛtam jñānam tena muhyanti jantavaḥ ||

morph.gloss: not (na + ā- → nā-)
to take, accept, receive (ādatte: present middle 3rd sg. 'takes, accepts')
anyone, someone (kasyacit: gen. sg. indefinite 'of anyone')
sin, evil (pāpam: acc. sg., object of ādatte)
not
and (ca + e- → cai-)
indeed, likewise
a good deed, merit (sukṛtam: acc. sg., object of ādatte, parallel to pāpam)
the all-pervading one, the lord (nom. sg., subject, referring to the self; cf. prabhuḥ of v.14)
ignorance (ajñānena: instr. sg. 'by ignorance')
to cover, veil (āvṛta: past participle 'covered, veiled', nom. sg. neut., agreeing with jñānam; ajñānena + ā- → ajñānenā-)
knowledge (nom. sg. neut., subject)
that, it (tena: instr. sg. 'by that [ignorance]')
to be deluded, confused (muhyanti: present 3rd pl.)
a creature, a being (nom. pl., subject of muhyanti)

sentences.l: Takes-not of-anyone sin, and-not, indeed, merit, the-all-pervading-one; by-ignorance covered [is] knowledge — by-that are-deluded creatures.
sentences.i: The all-pervading self takes on the sin of no one, nor his merit either; knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by that beings are deluded.
sentences.n: Vibhuḥ, 'the all-pervading one', echoes prabhuḥ of verse 14, both naming the self's non-involvement in the moral weight of action. The second half turns to explain ordinary confusion: ajñānena āvṛtaṃ jñānam, 'knowledge covered by ignorance', is why jantavaḥ, 'creatures', are deluded — the veil that the light-simile of the next verse removes.

sentences.t:
ज्ञानेन तु तदज्ञानं येषां नाशितमात्मनः ।
तेषामादित्यवज्ज्ञानं प्रकाशयति तत्परम् ॥
sentences.tr:
jñānena tu tat ajñānam yeṣām nāśitam ātmanaḥ |
teṣām āditya-vat jñānam prakāśayati tat param ||

morph.gloss: knowledge (instr. sg. 'by knowledge')
but, however
that (tat: nom. sg. neut., in apposition to ajñānam; -t + a- → -d a-)
ignorance (ajñānam: nom. sg. neut., subject of nāśitam)
who (yeṣām: gen. pl. relative 'of whom, for whom')
to destroy (causative nāśayati; nāśitam: past participle 'destroyed', nom. sg. neut., agreeing with ajñānam)
self (ātmanaḥ: gen. sg. 'of the self, their own')
that, they (teṣām: gen. pl. 'for them, of them')
the sun (āditya-vat: adverbial with -vat, 'like the sun')
knowledge (jñānam: nom. sg. neut., subject of prakāśayati; -vat + j- → -vajj-)
to shine forth, illumine (causative prakāśayati: present 3rd sg. 'illumines, reveals')
that (referring to the supreme reality)
supreme, the highest (tat param: 'that supreme [reality]', acc. sg. neut., object of prakāśayati)

sentences.l: By-knowledge, however, that ignorance of-whom [has been] destroyed, of-their-own self; for-them, like-the-sun, knowledge illumines that supreme.
sentences.i: But for those whose ignorance of the self has been destroyed by knowledge, their knowledge, like the sun, illumines that supreme reality.
sentences.n: Āditya-vat, 'like the sun', answers verse 15's covering ignorance with the chapter's light-image (compare 4.37's fire-image, jñānāgniḥ ... bhasmasāt kurute); tat param, 'that supreme [reality]', names what is revealed once ignorance of one's own self (ātmanaḥ) is destroyed by knowledge.

sentences.t:
तद्बुद्धयस्तदात्मानस्तन्निष्ठास्तत्परायणाः ।
गच्छन्त्यपुनरावृत्तिं ज्ञाननिर्धूतकल्मषाः ॥
sentences.tr:
tad-buddhayaḥ tad-ātmānaḥ tan-niṣṭhāḥ tat-parāyaṇāḥ |
gacchanti apunar-āvṛttim jñāna-nirdhūta-kalmaṣāḥ ||

morph.gloss: that, brahman (first member in each compound, referring to brahman)
intellect, understanding (tad-buddhi: 'whose understanding is fixed on that', buddhayaḥ: nom. pl.; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
that (repeated)
self (tad-ātman: 'whose mind is that', ātmānaḥ: nom. pl.; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
that (repeated, tan- before n-)
foundation, ground, steadfastness (tan-niṣṭhā: 'grounded in that', niṣṭhāḥ: nom. pl.; -āḥ + t- → -ās t-)
that (repeated)
wholly devoted to, intent upon (tat-parāyaṇa: 'devoted to that', nom. pl., subject of gacchanti)
to go (gacchanti: present 3rd pl. 'they go'; -i + a- → -y a-)
non-return (apunarāvṛtti: acc. sg. fem., object of gacchanti, 'to non-return, no rebirth')
knowledge (first compound member)
to shake off, remove (nirdhūta: past participle, second compound member)
sin, taint (jñāna-nirdhūta-kalmaṣa: 'whose sins are shaken off by knowledge', nom. pl.)

sentences.l: Whose-understanding-is-that, whose-self-is-that, whose-ground-is-that, whose-devotion-is-that — they-go to-non-return, whose-sins-are-removed-by-knowledge.
sentences.i: Those whose understanding, mind, foundation, and whole devotion are fixed on that [brahman], go to a state from which there is no return, their sins washed away by knowledge.
sentences.n: Four parallel tad-compounds (tad-buddhayaḥ, tad-ātmānaḥ, tan-niṣṭhāḥ, tat-parāyaṇāḥ) describe total absorption in brahman ('that') by four faculties in turn; apunarāvṛttim, 'to non-return', names final liberation from rebirth — the same idea of non-return recurs later, in different words (na nivartante at 8.21, 15.4, 15.6; anāvṛttim at 8.26), though the compound apunarāvṛtti itself is not repeated — and is distinct from but related to 4.9's na sa ... punarjanma naiti.

sentences.t:
विद्याविनयसंपन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि ।
शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः ॥
sentences.tr:
vidyā-vinaya-sampanne brāhmaṇe gavi hastini |
śuni ca eva śva-pāke ca paṇḍitāḥ sama-darśinaḥ ||

morph.gloss: learning, knowledge (first compound member)
humility, discipline, good conduct (second compound member)
endowed with, possessed of (vidyā-vinaya-sampanna: 'endowed with learning and humility', loc. sg., agreeing with brāhmaṇe)
a brahmin (loc. sg.)
cow, ox (loc. sg. 'in a cow')
elephant (loc. sg.)
dog (śuni: loc. sg.)
and (ca + e- → cai-)
indeed, even
dog (first compound member)
cooking (śva-pāka: 'dog-cooker', a term for an outcaste; loc. sg.)
and
the wise, the learned (nom. pl., subject)
equal, the same (first compound member)
seeing (sama-darśin: 'seeing with an equal eye', nom. pl., predicate)

sentences.l: In-a-brahmin-endowed-with-learning-and-humility, in-a-cow, in-an-elephant, and-indeed in-a-dog, and in-an-outcaste — the-wise [are] of-equal-vision.
sentences.i: The wise see with an equal eye a learned and humble brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste.
sentences.n: This famous verse spans the whole human and animal range — from a learned, humble brahmin down through a cow and elephant to a dog and a śvapāka, 'dog-cooker' (a term for the lowest outcaste) — to state the sage's sama-darśana, 'equal vision', grounded not in outward rank but in the one brahman underlying every form, as the next verse explains.

sentences.t:
इहैव तैर्जितः सर्गो येषां साम्ये स्थितं मनः ।
निर्दोषं हि समं ब्रह्म तस्माद्ब्रह्मणि ते स्थिताः ॥
sentences.tr:
iha eva taiḥ jitaḥ sargaḥ yeṣām sāmye sthitam manaḥ |
nirdoṣam hi samam brahma tasmāt brahmaṇi te sthitāḥ ||

morph.gloss: here, in this world, in this very life (iha + e- → ihai-)
even, indeed
they (taiḥ: instr. pl. 'by them'; -aiḥ + j- → -air j-)
to conquer (jita: past participle 'conquered', nom. sg., agreeing with sargaḥ)
creation, birth, the cycle of rebirth (nom. sg., subject; -aḥ before y- → -o)
who (yeṣām: gen. pl. relative 'whose')
sameness, equality, equanimity (loc. sg.)
to stand, be established (sthita: past participle 'established, fixed', nom. sg. neut., agreeing with manaḥ)
mind (nom. sg. neut., subject of sthitam)
faultless, without blemish (nom. sg. neut., predicate agreeing with brahma)
for, indeed
equal, the same (nom. sg. neut., predicate)
brahman (nom. sg. neut., subject, kept untranslated)
that (tasmāt: abl. sg. 'therefore'; -t + b- → -d b-)
brahman (brahmaṇi: loc. sg. 'in brahman', kept untranslated)
they (nom. pl.)
to stand, be established (sthita: past participle 'established', nom. pl., predicate 'are established')

sentences.l: Even-here indeed by-them [is] conquered the-worldly-cycle, by-whom in-sameness [is] established the-mind; faultless indeed, the-same, [is] brahman — therefore in-brahman they [are] established.
sentences.i: Even in this life, rebirth is conquered by those whose mind is fixed in equanimity; for brahman is faultless and the same everywhere, and therefore they are established in brahman.
sentences.n: Ihaiva, 'even here, in this very life', announces the poem's doctrine of liberation attainable while still embodied, developed further in verses 24-26; sargaḥ, 'the round of birth', is conquered by sāmye sthitaṃ manaḥ, 'a mind established in sameness', because brahman itself is sama, 'the same [everywhere]' — the ground for the samadarśana of verse 18.

sentences.t:
न प्रहृष्येत्प्रियं प्राप्य नोद्विजेत्प्राप्य चाप्रियम् ।
स्थिरबुद्धिरसंमूढो ब्रह्मविद्ब्रह्मणि स्थितः ॥
sentences.tr:
na prahṛṣyet priyam prāpya na udvijet prāpya ca apriyam |
sthira-buddhiḥ asammūḍhaḥ brahma-vit brahmaṇi sthitaḥ ||

morph.gloss: not
to rejoice, exult (prahṛṣyet: optative 3rd sg. 'should rejoice')
dear, pleasant (priyam: acc. sg. neut., object of prāpya, 'on obtaining the pleasant')
to obtain, attain (prāpya: gerund 'having obtained')
not (na + u- → no-)
to be agitated, recoil, be repelled (udvijet: optative 3rd sg. 'should be agitated, repelled')
to obtain (prāpya: gerund 'having obtained', repeated)
and (ca + a- → cā-)
unpleasant, disagreeable (apriyam: acc. sg. neut., object of the second prāpya)
steady, firm (first compound member)
intellect, understanding (sthira-buddhi: 'of steady intellect', buddhiḥ: nom. sg.; -iḥ + a- → -ir a-)
undeluded, unconfused (asammūḍhaḥ: nom. sg.; -aḥ before b- → -o)
brahman (first compound member, kept untranslated)
knowing (vit: 'a knower', brahma-vit: 'a knower of brahman', nom. sg.; -t + b- → -d b-)
brahman (brahmaṇi: loc. sg. 'in brahman', kept untranslated)
to stand, be established (sthita: past participle 'established', nom. sg., predicate)

sentences.l: Not should-he-rejoice, the-pleasant having-obtained; not should-he-be-agitated, having-obtained, and, the-unpleasant; of-steady-intellect, undeluded, a-knower-of-brahman, in-brahman established.
sentences.i: He should not rejoice on obtaining what is pleasant, nor be agitated on obtaining what is unpleasant; steady in understanding, undeluded, a knower of brahman, he is established in brahman.
sentences.n: This makes verse 19's sāmya, 'evenness', concrete as equanimity toward priyam and apriyam, 'the pleasant and the unpleasant' (cf. 2.14's śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha); brahma-vid brahmaṇi sthitaḥ, 'a knower of brahman established in brahman', closes the description of samadarśana begun at verse 18 and opens into the inward joy described in verses 21-23.

sentences.t:
बाह्यस्पर्शेष्वसक्तात्मा विन्दत्यात्मनि यत् सुखम् ।
स ब्रह्मयोगयुक्तात्मा सुखमक्षयमश्नुते ॥
sentences.tr:
bāhya-sparśeṣu asakta-ātmā vindati ātmani yat sukham |
saḥ brahma-yoga-yukta-ātmā sukham akṣayam aśnute ||

morph.gloss: external, outer (first compound member)
contact, touch (bāhya-sparśa: 'external contact', sparśeṣu: loc. pl. 'in external contacts'; -eṣu + a- → -eṣva-)
unattached (asakta: past participle, first member)
self (asakta-ātman: 'whose self is unattached', nom. sg.; asakta + ātmā → asaktātmā)
to find (vindati: present 3rd sg. 'finds'; -i + ā- → -y ā-)
self (ātmani: loc. sg. 'in the self')
which (acc. sg. neut. relative, object of vindati)
happiness (acc. sg. neut., in apposition to yat)
that, he (nom. sg. masc.)
brahman (first compound member, kept untranslated)
yoga, discipline (brahma-yoga: 'the discipline [that unites one] with brahman', second member)
joined, united (third member)
self (brahma-yoga-yukta-ātman: 'whose self is united through the discipline of brahman', nom. sg., subject)
happiness (sukham: acc. sg., object of aśnute)
imperishable, undecaying (akṣayam: acc. sg., agreeing with sukham)
to obtain, enjoy, partake of (aśnute: present middle 3rd sg. 'enjoys')

sentences.l: In-external-contacts, of-unattached-self, he-finds in-the-self what happiness; he, of-self-united-through-the-discipline-of-brahman, happiness imperishable enjoys.
sentences.i: His self unattached to external contacts, he finds the happiness that is within the self; united with brahman through discipline, he enjoys imperishable happiness.
sentences.n: Bāhya-sparśa, '[sense-]contact with external objects', is what such a person is asakta, 'unattached' to; the happiness he instead finds is ātmani, 'within the self', not from outer contact — the point developed by contrast in the next two verses.

sentences.t:
ये हि संस्पर्शजा भोगा दुःखयोनय एव ते ।
आद्यन्तवन्तः कौन्तेय न तेषु रमते बुधः ॥
sentences.tr:
ye hi saṃsparśa-jāḥ bhogāḥ duḥkha-yonayaḥ eva te |
ādi-anta-vantaḥ kaunteya na teṣu ramate budhaḥ ||

morph.gloss: which (nom. pl. masc. relative)
indeed, for

sentences.l: Which indeed contact-born pleasures, sources-of-suffering indeed they; having-beginning-and-end, O son-of-Kuntī — not in-them delights the-wise-one.
sentences.i: The pleasures that arise from sense-contact are truly sources of suffering, Kaunteya; they have a beginning and an end, and the wise do not delight in them.
sentences.n: Kaunteya, 'son of Kuntī', a new epithet of Arjuna in this chapter (translated on this first use, given as the name thereafter, per convention). Saṃsparśajā bhogāḥ, 'pleasures born of [sense-]contact', are duḥkha-yonayaḥ, 'sources of suffering', precisely because ādyantavantaḥ, 'having a beginning and an end' — unlike the akṣayaṃ sukham, 'imperishable happiness', of verse 21.

sentences.l: Is-able, even-here, who to-endure, before-the-release-of-the-body, the-impulse-arising-from-desire-and-anger — he [is] disciplined, he [is] happy, [that] man.
sentences.i: The man who is able, in this very life, to withstand the force that arises from desire and anger, before he leaves the body — he is disciplined, and he is a happy man.
sentences.n: Prāk śarīra-vimokṣaṇāt, 'before the release of the body', i.e. before death, while still alive, continues the ihaiva, 'even here', theme of verse 19; kāma-krodha-udbhavaṃ vegam, 'the force arising from desire and anger', recalls the chain from kāma to krodha traced at 2.62-63, here mastered rather than merely avoided.

sentences.l: Who inwardly-happy, inwardly-rejoicing, likewise inwardly-luminous indeed, who — he, the-yogin, brahman-extinction, become-brahman, attains.
sentences.i: The yogin who is happy within, who rejoices within, and who has light within, becomes one with brahman and attains extinction in brahman.
sentences.n: This introduces brahma-nirvāṇam, 'extinction, liberation in brahman', a term repeated at verses 25 and 26; the threefold antar-, 'inward', compounds (antaḥsukhaḥ, antarārāmaḥ, antarjyotiḥ) describe a happiness wholly independent of outer objects, continuing verse 21's bāhya-sparśeṣu asaktātmā. The relative pronoun yaḥ is stylistically repeated across the long list of qualities (yo 'ntaḥsukho ... yaḥ), resumed by sa in the second line.

sentences.l: Obtain brahman-extinction the-sages, whose-sins-are-destroyed; whose-doubt-is-cut-off, whose-self-is-restrained, in-the-welfare-of-all-beings delighting.
sentences.i: The sages whose sins are destroyed, whose doubts are cut away, whose selves are restrained, and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain extinction in brahman.
sentences.n: Chinna-dvaidhāḥ, 'whose duality/doubt is severed', recalls the doubt-cutting of 4.42 (chittvainaṃ saṃśayam) with the broader term dvaidha, 'dividedness'; sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ, 'devoted to the welfare of all beings', adds an active dimension of compassion alongside the contemplative brahma-nirvāṇa.

abhitaḥ brahma-nirvāṇam vartate vidita-ātmanām ||

sentences.l: Of-those-freed-from-desire-and-anger, of-ascetics, of-restrained-mind — close-at-hand, brahman-extinction exists, for-those-who-have-known-the-self.
sentences.i: For ascetics who are free of desire and anger, whose minds are restrained and who have known the self, extinction in brahman is close at hand.
sentences.n: This closes the three-verse brahma-nirvāṇa sequence (24-26); abhitaḥ is glossed by Śaṅkara here as 'on both sides' — jīvataḥ ca mṛtasya ca, 'whether living or dead' — so that brahma-nirvāṇa belongs to the self-knower both in life and after death, alongside the more general adverbial sense 'close at hand, on every side'; either way it ties the triad back to verse 19's ihaiva — liberation already attainable in this very life, not deferred to another.

sentences.i: Shutting out external sense-contacts, fixing the eyes between the eyebrows, and making the outward and downward breaths move evenly within the nostrils,
sentences.n: This opens a description of yogic posture completed in verse 28: bahir bāhyān sparśān kṛtvā, 'having put external contacts outside', and cakṣuḥ ... antare bhruvoḥ, 'the eye between the eyebrows' (the classical fixed gaze-point), together with prāṇāpānau samau, 'the two breaths made even', describe a breath-discipline related to the breath-sacrifices catalogued at 4.29-30, here practiced as a direct path to liberation.

sentences.l: Whose-senses-mind-and-intellect-are-restrained, the-sage, intent-on-liberation; from-whom-desire-fear-and-anger-have-departed, who — always liberated indeed [is] he.
sentences.i: The sage whose senses, mind and intellect are restrained, and who is intent on liberation, who has cast off desire, fear and anger — he is forever liberated.
sentences.n: This completes the sentence begun at verse 27, naming the goal directly as mokṣa-parāyaṇaḥ, 'intent on liberation'; vigata-icchā-bhaya-krodhaḥ recasts verse 26's kāma-krodha-viyuktānām with icchā, 'desire, wish', and fear now added. Sadā mukta eva saḥ, 'he is ever liberated indeed', is the main predicate closing the two-verse sentence.

suhṛdam sarva-bhūtānām jñātvā mām śāntim ṛcchati ||

sentences.l: The-enjoyer of-sacrifices-and-austerities, the-great-lord-of-all-worlds, the-friend of-all-beings, having-known me — peace he-attains.
sentences.i: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.
sentences.n: The chapter's closing verse names Kṛṣṇa in three roles that gather much of what has come before: bhoktāraṃ yajña-tapasām, 'enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities' (recalling the sacrifice-catalogue of 4.24-32), sarva-loka-mahā-īśvaram, 'great lord of all worlds' (echoing 4.6's bhūtānām īśvaraḥ), and suhṛdaṃ sarva-bhūtānām, 'friend of all beings' (a new, warmer epithet, taken up again at 9.18 and 11.44). Jñātvā mām ... śāntim ṛcchati, 'knowing me, he attains peace', closes the chapter as 4.9's mām eti closed the last, on the same note that opens the yoga-chapters to come.

about: Chapter 5 answers the question Arjuna opens it with: whether renunciation of action or the yoga of action is better. Kṛṣṇa ranks karma-yoga slightly ahead, but only to collapse the apparent opposition — sāṃkhya and yoga, rightly practiced, yield the same fruit, and true renunciation turns out to be an inward freedom from hatred and desire, not outward abstention from acts, indeed one that is hard to reach without yoga first. The chapter's central figure is the disciplined yogin who acts with body, mind and senses yet remains untouched, like a lotus-leaf on water, because he has surrendered his actions and their fruit; a run of verses lists the ordinary bodily and sense-functions such a person still performs while holding that it is the senses, not the self, that move among their objects. From there the chapter turns to the metaphysics behind this freedom: the self neither creates agency nor claims sin or merit, and ignorance alone is what veils knowledge, which knowledge then dispels like sunlight. The wise, seeing the one brahman equally in a learned brahmin and an outcaste, in a cow and a dog, become steady amid pleasure and pain and find a happiness that owes nothing to outer contact. Three closing verses describe the yogin who has turned wholly inward as attaining brahma-nirvāṇa — extinction, or liberation, in brahman — available already in this life to whoever has cut away doubt, desire and anger. The chapter closes with a description of the breath-controlled ascetic and a final image of Kṛṣṇa himself as the enjoyer of all sacrifice, the great lord of all worlds, and the friend of every being, knowing whom is the way to peace.
